Recovery after a **periacetabular osteotomy (PAO)** is usually measured in **months, not weeks**. A typical overall timeline is:

- **Hospital stay:** about **1–5 days**, commonly around **2–4 days**. ([yalemedicine.org](https://www.yalemedicine.org/conditions/periacetabular-osteotomy-pao?utm_source=openai))
- **Protected or limited weight-bearing with crutches/walker:** often **about 6–8 weeks**, and sometimes **8–12 weeks** until bone healing and muscle function are adequate. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1302/1863-2548.12.180068?utm_source=openai))
- **Return to desk/school-type activities:** often **around 6–12 weeks**, depending on pain, energy, and whether you can avoid a lot of walking. This is a general clinical expectation; exact timing varies by surgeon protocol and job demands. ([healthcare.utah.edu](https://healthcare.utah.edu/orthopaedics/specialties/hip-pain/periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))
- **More normal day-to-day function:** often **3–6 months**. ([myhssmedia.hss.edu](https://myhssmedia.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))
- **Full recovery / higher-level sports recovery:** commonly **6–12 months**. ([myhssmedia.hss.edu](https://myhssmedia.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))

A short version: many people feel the recovery is **rough for the first 6–8 weeks**, noticeably better by **3 months**, and still improving for **6–12 months**. ([healthcare.utah.edu](https://healthcare.utah.edu/orthopaedics/specialties/hip-pain/periacetabular-osteotomy/recovery?utm_source=openai))

A few things can make it longer:
- having **additional procedures** done at the same time, such as labral repair or femoral osteotomy,
- slower bone healing,
- higher pain levels,
- physically demanding work. ([yalemedicine.org](https://www.yalemedicine.org/conditions/periacetabular-osteotomy-pao?utm_source=openai))

Because this is a medical question, the safest answer is that **your surgeon’s protocol is the one that matters most**; PAO recovery plans vary quite a bit by technique and what was repaired. Recovery from a periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) usually takes about **6 months to a year**. Most people can do everyday activities again by around 3 months, and the hip can keep getting stronger for up to 2 years. One hospital says it typically expects recovery to take about six months, but you will see continued improvements in your mobility and strength for up to two years after surgery. University of Utah Health says it usually takes 9–12 months to feel fully recovered.

**Typical timeline**

- **In the hospital:** Stays usually last 2 to 4 days, depending on the hospital. You will start physical therapy the day after surgery. Plan on having someone to take care of you 24/7 for the first week.
- **Weeks 0–6:** Walk with crutches (partial weight bearing), and keep your wound clean. Many centers say crutches must be used for 6 to 8 weeks.
- **Weeks 6–12:** Transition to one cane or crutch as instructed by your provider. You may start gentle stretching or strengthening exercises.
- **Around 3 months:** Return to work part time or full time as tolerated. A recent patient survey found that most patients went back to school and work within 12 weeks, and 55% were driving again within 6 weeks.
- **6 months and later:** You may return to full activity (when the bone cuts are completely healed) except for running/jumping activities. Most people can resume athletics between 6 to 12 months.

**Why you shouldn't rush:** One study compared a faster rehab program with a standard one. Patients on the faster program walked without support sooner (4.2 months and 6.9 months), but postoperative pelvic fracture rates were unacceptably high in patients with this protocol. It's important to follow your surgeon's weight-bearing limits.

You'll also have regular check-ups. Patients typically see their provider two weeks after surgery, then again at six weeks for X-rays, and again at three months, six months, one year. answer.answerText:
Recovery from **rotator cuff surgery** usually takes **4 to 6 months**, but it can be **6 to 12 months** for a large or massive tear. The tendon typically takes about **6 to 8 weeks** to heal back to the bone. ([medlineplus.gov](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))

A typical timeline is:

- **First 4–6 weeks:** sling/immobilizer, limited shoulder use. ([medlineplus.gov](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))
- **Around 6–8 weeks:** early healing of the repair; physical therapy is often ongoing. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/torn-rotator-cuff-surgery?utm_source=openai))
- **About 3 months:** many people can return to most routine activities. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/torn-rotator-cuff-surgery?utm_source=openai))
- **4–6 months:** common range for fuller recovery after smaller to larger tears. ([medlineplus.gov](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))
- **6–12 months:** sometimes needed for severe or massive tears or slower rehab progress. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/torn-rotator-cuff-surgery?utm_source=openai))

Recovery time depends on the **size of the tear**, the **type of repair**, your **age**, whether you **smoke**, and how closely you follow **physical therapy and activity restrictions**. ([medlineplus.gov](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/007207.htm?utm_source=openai))
